## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so the default setup almost never produces an exact build within 131k steps. Two things could cause this. First, too few samples: 32 updates of 4,096 steps is very little for a credit-assignment problem with about 1,000 actions. Second, the wrong features: the column stem mixes all layers together, so it is hard for it to learn the key test for a placement, which is whether the footprint lands at layer L = max height and every cell of the footprint at layer L is a missing target cell. This round is close to a factorial design. Candidate 1 keeps the baseline network and changes only the recipe (fewer PPO epochs, so more samples and more updates). Candidates 2 and 3 use a new per-layer network with a similar FLOP cost under two levels of epoch reduction. Comparing 1 with 2 isolates the architecture, and comparing 2 with 3 isolates the epochs-versus-samples trade-off.

### Round 2
All four trials so far, including the starting architecture, scored exactly 0, and so did training success. So neither sample count (1, 2 and 4 PPO epochs) nor the per-layer structure changed anything we can measure. When everything is zero, a training failure of the whole system is more likely than a capacity limit. My leading guess is early collapse onto DONE. A random placement has negative expected reward (cells outside the target, minus 0.01), while DONE gives 0. DONE is a single action that keeps getting a positive advantage, so it may take over before correct placement is learned across 256 actions. And without DONE after a complete build, extra bricks get placed and the build is never exact. This round shares one exploration-friendly recipe (ent 0.03, gamma 0.99, lambda 0.95, 2 epochs) across three candidates: the baseline network (recipe effect), a DONE-bias prior (collapse test), and a generic deeper network with learned 3x3 heads (architecture effect, and robust if the anchor convention differs from the stated one).

### Round 3
All six trials score exactly 0, and so does training success in the last 10% of training. The trials varied sample count (up to 409k steps), PPO epochs, exploration, gamma, a DONE prior, depth, learned 3x3 heads and a per-layer structure. Because every one of them is 0, seed noise does not explain it, and generic recipe or capacity changes are not the cause. The task warns that the world may differ from its description. The most likely problem is that the action layout does not match the stated convention, for example transposed y and x, reflected anchors, or a different type or cell ordering. Every head tried so far maps cell (y,x) to action (t,y,x) through convolution, which shifts with the input and cannot learn a transposition or a permutation of actions. This round tests heads that make no assumption about the layout: a dense head on a conv trunk, a pure MLP, and a conv head that can learn to mix in flipped or transposed copies of its logit maps.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on both seeds, and training success was also 0. The trials covered more samples, more exploration, a DONE prior, deeper nets, dense and MLP heads, and flip or transpose heads, so no single idea has shown a signal. One factor has gone unnoticed: every recipe so far cut the number of gradient steps. The default makes 32 updates × 4 epochs × 32 minibatches = 4,096 steps; r1c1 made about 1,900 and r1c3 about 1,660. Getting an exact build depends on precise per-anchor decisions about where each brick lands, which may need many small, low-noise updates rather than more fresh samples. In this final round I test (a) the baseline with about 2× the gradient steps on 64-sample minibatches; (b) a head whose learned convolution has the brick's own footprint as its kernel, so it sees each covered cell individually, plus that recipe; (c) global self-attention so every cell sees the whole design, to help with ordering and with choosing DONE.
